title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
Can physics-informed neural networks compete with a classical numerical solver for option pricing? In this project, I implemented and compared three approaches to pricing European call options: Crank–Nicolson, a physics-informed neural network (PINN), and a physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network (PIKAN).
For the one-dimensional Black–Scholes problem tested, Crank–Nicolson achieved the lowest pricing errors and shortest runtime. PIKAN improved substantially on the baseline PINN’s accuracy, but required considerably more training time.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
Can physics-informed neural networks compete with a classical numerical solver for option pricing? In this project, I implemented and compared three approaches to pricing European call options: Crank–Nicolson, a physics-informed neural network (PINN), and a physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network (PIKAN).
For the one-dimensional Black–Scholes problem tested, Crank–Nicolson achieved the lowest pricing errors and shortest runtime. PIKAN improved substantially on the baseline PINN’s accuracy, but required considerably more training time.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
Why this problem?
Black–Scholes provides a useful controlled benchmark because European call prices have an analytical solution. This makes it possible to measure approximation errors directly rather than compare numerical methods against another approximate reference.
The aim was to investigate the accuracy and computational cost of physics-informed learning in a setting where a strong classical method already exists.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
How I compared the methods
Crank–Nicolson approximates the pricing equation on a grid, solving a tridiagonal linear system at each time step. The PINN instead represents the price function with a multilayer perceptron, trained to satisfy the differential equation and its initial and boundary conditions. The PIKAN uses the same physics-informed principle with a spline-based Kolmogorov–Arnold network.
For the main experiment, I used a strike price of 100, a one-year maturity, a 5% risk-free rate and 20% volatility. All methods were assessed against analytical prices on the same 100 × 50 evaluation grid.
I evaluated several PINN configurations and two PIKAN training lengths. Performance measures included root mean squared error (RMSE), maximum absolute error, relative L2 error and runtime.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
Main findings
In the main comparison, Crank–Nicolson achieved an RMSE of approximately 0.0098 in 0.29 seconds. The baseline PINN achieved approximately 0.501 in 33.7 seconds, while the PIKAN trained for 3,000 epochs achieved approximately 0.0581 in 257.6 seconds.
The PIKAN therefore offered a clear accuracy improvement over the baseline PINN, although Crank–Nicolson remained both faster and more accurate. Increasing PINN width or adding a learning-rate scheduler did not consistently improve performance, illustrating the importance of testing implementation choices.

Sensitivity to volatility
In a separate sensitivity experiment, I tested volatility values from 10% to 40%. Crank–Nicolson retained the lowest RMSE at every tested value, and PIKAN consistently improved on the baseline PINN.



Pricing RMSE across four volatility assumptions in the sensitivity experiment. Crank–Nicolson achieved the lowest error at each tested value.


Errors increased noticeably for both Crank–Nicolson and PIKAN at 40% volatility. This motivates further investigation of resolution, boundary effects and training choices.
The runtime comparison shows that PIKAN’s improvement over the baseline PINN came at substantial computational cost. Crank–Nicolson runtimes were positive but too small to distinguish clearly on the plotted scale.



Recorded runtime across four volatility assumptions. Neural-network training was substantially more expensive than the Crank–Nicolson solve.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
What I learned and limitations
The main lesson was the value of a strong numerical baseline. Learning the overall shape of a price surface is not sufficient: accuracy and computational cost must also justify the approach.
These results concern the implementations and problem tested. The neural models differed in parameter counts, training points and training lengths, so the comparison does not isolate architecture alone. Experiments used a laptop without a dedicated CUDA-enabled GPU, and fixed seeds rather than repeated trials across multiple seeds. Reported runtimes concern solving or training, rather than a separate inference-speed benchmark.
The study excludes stochastic volatility, dividends and early exercise. A natural extension is to investigate how the accuracy–cost trade-off changes as problem dimensionality increases, using matched computational budgets and repeated runs.
